## Where session 1 left off

::: {.notes}
Session 1 built vocabulary. This session is about deciding when and how to apply it.
Name the handoff from Jackson explicitly and keep it to thirty seconds.
:::

---

## ETL systems are just software

::: {.notes}
Nothing meaningfully distinguishes a pipeline from a web app. The users are often other
systems or other developers, which removes some pressures but adds none that are special.
So general design principles apply unchanged.
:::

---

## "Design" vs "Architecture"

::: {.notes}
Treat them as equivalent for this hour. The distinction is a topic for another session and
doesn't earn its keep at the scale of systems we build. Say this once, then stop
re-litigating it.
:::

---

## What is design?

::: {.notes}
The decisions and elements that determine how software satisfies its requirements within
its constraints: components and responsibilities, interfaces and relationships, algorithms
and data representations, and the policies governing operation and evolution.
:::

---

## Every system has an architecture

::: {.notes}
Whether or not anyone intended one. Architecture is also recursive and relative to a
boundary: a system can express very different principles than its components, and you can
reason about a component independently of its parent.
:::

---

## The design is what runs

::: {.notes}
Design is embodied by the running code and deployed system, not by modules, files, or
documentation. Static descriptions drift from the realized architecture. This is also what
separates application architecture from deployment architecture.
:::

---

## What design is not

::: {.notes}
Not diagrams, docs, technology choices, "service oriented", cloud resources, or specific
patterns. Those express or support a design. Fast slide, read the list, move on.
:::

---

## Design is cost and benefit under uncertainty

::: {.notes}
It's imprecise and hard. It may not be worth the effort, and deciding not to design
deliberately is itself a design decision. Proficiency comes from practice and failure.
AI still can't do it consistently well, which is the honest reason to learn it.
:::

---

## [PRINCIPLES]{.tier} <br>

::: {.notes}
Divider. Make the asymmetry explicit before the blocks start: three of these decide where
boundaries go, one decides what a boundary promises. Idempotency is the odd one out, and
that's why it comes first and then keeps reappearing.
:::

---

## Idempotency

::: {.notes}
Sharpen past session 1: multiple calls have the same effect on system state as a single
call. It says nothing about the return value. That second half is the part people get
wrong.
:::

---

## Where you have already met it

::: {.notes}
`set.add`, `dict.update`, `min`/`max`; HTTP `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE`; Bicep and Terraform.
Against: `list.append`, `POST`, `PATCH`, and most functions you write. Recognition, not
definition.
:::

---

## The devil is in the implementation details

::: {.fail}
[Symptom:]{.lbl} a `GET` handler that writes on every request, or a `__setitem__` that
appends to a list it also keys.

[That's:]{.lbl} an interface whose stated guarantee and actual behavior have diverged.
:::

::: {.notes}
Nothing stops you from implementing a non-idempotent `GET`. The convention is the contract,
and callers will design against the convention. Keep this short, it's a setup for the
information hiding block.
:::

---

## Idempotency in SQL

::: {.notes}
Trivially idempotent: `SELECT`, and `UPDATE`/`DELETE` with a `WHERE`. Bought with syntax:
`CREATE OR REPLACE`, `IF NOT EXISTS`, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`.
The most directly applicable slide in this block for an ETL audience.
:::

---

## Retry logic you don't have to write

::: {.maps}
**Maps to the requirement:** a guarantee at the boundary removes branching from every
caller. Compare the two `save_names` implementations: the cleanup loop in the caller
disappears entirely.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff slide. Walk the non-idempotent caller first so the cleanup loop is
visible, then the idempotent one. The trade-off is that complexity moved, it didn't vanish.
:::

---

## Idempotency: the trade-off

::: {.notes}
Usually harder to implement. Weigh the added effort against what downstream components can
absorb. For anything bigger than a single script, lean toward it.
:::

---

## Information hiding: decide what callers cannot see

::: {.notes}
Hiding implementation decisions from other components. The central idea of the session.
It narrows what you have to hold in your head while designing, which is most of its value.
:::

---

## `persistence.py` before you pick a database

::: {.notes}
Stub the interface other components depend on: `get_user()`, `query_landfills()`,
`upsert_reservoir_data()`. Callers don't depend on how data is stored. CSVs now, Postgres
later, without touching anything upstream.
:::

---

## The interface is where guarantees live

::: {.notes}
Callback, earned rather than ritual: `upsert_reservoir_data()` names an idempotent
operation. That one choice is simultaneously an information hiding decision and a promise
callers get to build on. This is the slide that justifies idempotency going first.
:::

---

## Delaying a decision is a design technique

::: {.notes}
If a design keeps a choice reversible, you decide later with more information. Schemas are
hard to change, so the interface that hides the schema is what buys you the option.
Procrastination with a purpose.
:::

---

## Insulating the system from a data provider

::: {.notes}
`GEMExtractionClient`, `CCReservoirsAPI`. When a provider changes its response format,
auth, or rate limiting, exactly one module changes. This is the concrete version of
"contain the change."
:::

---

## Information hiding: the trade-off

::: {.notes}
Mostly cognitive load during design, and compartmentalizing is genuinely awkward at first.
Of the four, this has the fewest trade-offs and the widest applicability, especially when
refactoring.
:::

---

## Single responsibility: group by reason for change

> Gather together the things that change for the same reasons.
> Separate things that change for different reasons.

::: {.notes}
Not "a function should do one thing" and not the Unix philosophy. It's a guide for grouping
capabilities. The connection to information hiding is tight: the decisions you hide are
usually the reasons something changes.
:::

---

## Modules and packages are the boundary you already have

::: {.notes}
In Python, modules and packages give you clear, inspectable boundaries to analyze through
this lens. You don't need new machinery. Adherence is a direction, not a gate: look at what
changed together over the last year to decide whether something should split.
:::

---

## Single responsibility: the trade-off

::: {.notes}
More subjective than the others, and more dependent on the domain and on a component's
relationships. Hardest of the four to argue about productively in a code review.
:::

---

## Dependency inversion: depend on stable abstractions

::: {.notes}
The apotheosis of information hiding: a `Protocol` has no implementation details at all.
Introduce this only as far as the examples need it, it's supporting technique rather than
headline.
:::

---

## Dependencies point inward, control flows outward

::: {.notes}
Dependencies point toward more abstract, higher-level components. The flow of control
generally runs opposite to the dependency direction, and that opposition is the "inversion."
Straightforward when an outside actor pushes in, like a CLI command or a request handler.
:::

---

## The anti-pattern: a provider's schema in your core

::: {.fail}
[Symptom:]{.lbl} an external API's field names and types appear in the module that holds
your business rules.

[That's:]{.lbl} core logic silently depending on a decision made by someone outside the
organization.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pay off the information hiding block here. This is the failure the whole session is
circling, and it's the one most likely to be sitting in a repo someone in the room owns.
:::

---

## Dependency inversion: the trade-off

::: {.notes}
Code volume and indirection. The one principle here where it's genuinely easy to overshoot,
so say that plainly rather than selling it.
:::

---

## The one habit worth changing

> Before you implement or change a component, decide how callers should use it,
> what they must be able to assume, and what they should be insulated from.

::: {.notes}
The single takeaway. Tie it back to the motivation slide: this is what contains changes,
makes results verifiable, and makes an unfamiliar repo navigable. On a small team, shared
boundaries and guarantees are what let us move between each other's projects.
:::

---

## Up next: a real package

::: {.notes}
Handoff to the second half. The principles above are abstract on purpose, because the
production code is where they get tested. Set up what to watch for rather than summarizing
again.
:::
